papers.title: Electrostatics: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on electrostatics, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A polythene rod becomes negatively charged when rubbed with wool because
questions.explanation:
Rubbing transfers electrons; the polythene gains them and becomes negative, the wool positive.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- protons move from the rod to the wool: Protons are fixed in the nucleus; only electrons move.
- electrons move from the rod to the wool: That would leave the rod positive.
- the rod creates new electrons: Charge is transferred, not created.

options.label: A
options.content: protons move from the rod to the wool

options.label: B
options.content: electrons move from the rod to the wool

options.label: D
options.content: electrons move from the wool to the rod

questions.stem: The only sure test that a body is charged is
questions.explanation:
Only like charges repel, so repulsion proves the body is charged.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- attraction by a charged rod: A charged rod also attracts an uncharged body, so attraction proves nothing.
- its ability to conduct electricity: Conduction shows a material is a conductor, not that it is charged.
- attraction by a magnet: Magnetism and static charge are different effects.

options.label: A
options.content: repulsion by a body with a known charge

questions.stem: A metal sphere is charged by induction using a positively charged rod. The charge on the sphere is
questions.explanation:
Electrons are attracted from earth to the sphere while the positive rod is near; the sphere ends up negative.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- positive: Induction gives the opposite charge to the inducing body.
- zero: After earthing and removing the earth, the sphere keeps a net charge.
- positive on one side and negative on the other only: That is the state before earthing; afterwards it has a net negative charge.

options.label: C
options.content: positive on one side and negative on the other only

questions.stem: Two point charges of 2 μC and 4 μC are 0.3 m apart in air. What is the force between them? (k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
questions.explanation:
$F = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^2} = \dfrac{9.0 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 4 \times 10^{-6}}{0.09} = 0.8\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.24 N: You divided by r instead of r².
- 0.4 N: You used 1 μC for one of the charges.
- 0.08 N: You divided by 0.9 instead of 0.09 (0.3² = 0.09).

questions.stem: If the distance between two point charges is doubled, the force between them
questions.explanation:
$F \propto 1/r^2$: doubling $r$ divides $F$ by 4.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- is halved: Coulomb's law is an inverse-square law.
- is doubled: Increasing distance weakens the force.
- is unchanged: The force depends on the distance.

questions.stem: Electric field lines
questions.explanation:
By convention field lines go from + to −, never cross, and crowd together where the field is strong.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- start on negative charges and end on positive charges: Field lines point the way a positive charge would move: away from +.
- can cross each other: Field lines never cross.
- are farther apart where the field is stronger: They are closer together where the field is stronger.

options.label: A
options.content: start on negative charges and end on positive charges

options.label: C
options.content: are farther apart where the field is stronger

options.label: D
options.content: start on positive charges and end on negative charges

questions.stem: How much work is done in moving a charge of 3 μC through a potential difference of 500 V?
questions.explanation:
$W = qV = 3 \times 10^{-6} \times 500 = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{J}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.75 mJ: W = qV here; ½QV is the energy stored in a capacitor.
- 1500 mJ: You treated μC as mC (10⁻³ C).
- 0.0015 mJ: That is the answer in joules; the options are in millijoules.

questions.stem: A lightning conductor protects a building mainly because
questions.explanation:
Point action neutralises the cloud's charge; if lightning strikes, the thick copper strip conducts it safely to earth.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- it attracts lightning away to another building: It protects the building it is on, by point action and a path to earth.
- it is made of an insulator: It is a thick conductor (copper).
- it stores the charge of the lightning: It conducts the charge to earth; it does not store it.

options.label: A
options.content: its sharp points discharge the cloud and it gives charge a safe path to earth

options.label: B
options.content: it attracts lightning away to another building

options.label: C
options.content: it is made of an insulator

options.label: D
options.content: it stores the charge of the lightning

papers.title: Capacitors: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on capacitors, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A 20 μF capacitor is connected to a 12 V battery. How much charge does it store?
questions.explanation:
$Q = CV = 20\ \mu\text{F} \times 12\ \text{V} = 240\ \mu\text{C}$ ($2.4 \times 10^{-4}$ C).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.67 μC: You divided C by V; Q = CV.
- 0.6 μC: You divided V by C; Q = CV.
- 32 μC: You added C and V instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: Capacitors of 3 μF and 6 μF are connected in series. What is their combined capacitance?
questions.explanation:
In series: $C = \dfrac{C_1C_2}{C_1 + C_2} = \dfrac{3 \times 6}{3 + 6} = 2\ \mu\text{F}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 9 μF: That is the combined capacitance in parallel.
- 4.5 μF: You averaged the capacitances.
- 18 μF: You multiplied without dividing by the sum.

questions.stem: Capacitors of 2 μF, 3 μF and 5 μF are connected in parallel. What is their combined capacitance?
questions.explanation:
In parallel: $C = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10\ \mu\text{F}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.97 μF: You used the series formula; in parallel capacitances add.
- 30 μF: You multiplied the capacitances.
- 5 μF: That is only the largest capacitor.

questions.stem: The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is increased by
questions.explanation:
$C = \varepsilon A/d$: a smaller gap, a larger area or a dielectric with higher permittivity increases C.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increasing the separation of the plates: C is inversely proportional to the separation.
- reducing the area of overlap of the plates: C is proportional to the area.
- replacing the dielectric with air: Air has a lower permittivity than most dielectrics.

options.label: A
options.content: increasing the separation of the plates

options.label: B
options.content: reducing the area of overlap of the plates

options.label: D
options.content: reducing the separation of the plates

questions.stem: What energy is stored in a 100 μF capacitor charged to 200 V?
questions.explanation:
$W = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 100 \times 10^{-6} \times 200^2 = 2\ \text{J}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4 J: You forgot the ½ in ½CV².
- 0.01 J: You used ½CV without squaring V.
- 0.02 J: That is the charge Q = CV in coulombs.

questions.stem: The SI unit of capacitance is the
questions.explanation:
Capacitance = charge ÷ p.d.; 1 farad = 1 coulomb per volt.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- coulomb: The coulomb is the unit of charge.
- henry: The henry is the unit of inductance.
- ohm: The ohm is the unit of resistance.

questions.stem: Capacitors of 4 μF and 12 μF in series are connected to a 16 V supply. What is the p.d. across the 4 μF capacitor?
questions.explanation:
$C = \dfrac{4 \times 12}{16} = 3\ \mu\text{F}$; $Q = 3 \times 16 = 48\ \mu\text{C}$; $V_4 = \dfrac{48}{4} = 12\ \text{V}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4 V: That is the p.d. across the 12 μF capacitor; the smaller capacitor takes the larger share.
- 8 V: In series, the p.d. is not shared equally.
- 16 V: The supply p.d. is shared between the two capacitors.

questions.stem: Inserting a dielectric between the plates of a charged, isolated capacitor
questions.explanation:
The dielectric becomes polarised and reduces the p.d. for the same charge, so C = Q/V increases.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- decreases its capacitance: A dielectric increases the capacitance by the factor εᵣ.
- has no effect on its capacitance: The permittivity of the gap changes, so C changes.
- makes it conduct: A dielectric is an insulator.

options.label: B
options.content: has no effect on its capacitance

papers.title: Current Electricity and Ohm's Law: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on current electricity and ohm's law, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A current of 0.5 A flows for 2 minutes. How much charge passes?
questions.explanation:
$Q = It = 0.5 \times 120 = 60\ \text{C}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1 C: You used 2 s instead of 120 s.
- 240 C: You divided the time by the current.
- 0.0042 C: You divided the current by the time.

questions.stem: A p.d. of 12 V across a resistor drives a current of 0.4 A. What is the resistance?
questions.explanation:
$R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{12}{0.4} = 30\ \Omega$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4.8 Ω: You multiplied V by I; R = V/I.
- 0.033 Ω: You divided I by V.
- 12.4 Ω: You added V and I.

questions.stem: Ohm's law holds for a metallic conductor provided
questions.explanation:
V ∝ I for a metal only while its temperature (and other physical conditions) stays the same.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the current is very large: Large currents heat the wire and change its resistance.
- the conductor is a semiconductor: Semiconductors do not obey Ohm's law.
- the p.d. is alternating: The condition is constant temperature (and other physical conditions).

questions.stem: A voltmeter is connected
questions.explanation:
A voltmeter goes across (in parallel with) the component and draws almost no current because its resistance is very high.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- in series with the component, and should have a very low resistance: That describes an ammeter.
- in parallel with the component, and should have a very low resistance: A low-resistance voltmeter would draw a large current and change the circuit.
- in series with the component, and should have a very high resistance: A voltmeter measures the p.d. across a component, so it goes in parallel.

options.label: A
options.content: in series with the component, and should have a very low resistance

options.label: B
options.content: in parallel with the component, and should have a very low resistance

options.label: C
options.content: in series with the component, and should have a very high resistance

options.label: D
options.content: in parallel with the component, and should have a very high resistance

questions.stem: A wire has a resistance of 8 Ω. What is the resistance of a wire of the same material that is twice as long and has twice the diameter?
questions.explanation:
$R \propto \dfrac{l}{A}$ and $A \propto d^2$: $R' = 8 \times \dfrac{2}{4} = 4\ \Omega$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 8 Ω: Doubling the diameter quadruples the area, which more than cancels doubling the length.
- 16 Ω: You doubled for the length but ignored the larger area.
- 2 Ω: Doubling the length doubles R; you divided by 4 twice.

questions.stem: A cell of e.m.f. 3.0 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to a 5 Ω resistor. What current flows?
questions.explanation:
$I = \dfrac{E}{R + r} = \dfrac{3.0}{5 + 1} = 0.5\ \text{A}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.6 A: You ignored the internal resistance.
- 3 A: You divided by the internal resistance only.
- 0.75 A: You subtracted the resistances.

questions.stem: A cell of e.m.f. 2.0 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω delivers 1.0 A. What is its terminal p.d.?
questions.explanation:
$V = E - Ir = 2.0 - 1.0 \times 0.5 = 1.5\ \text{V}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2.0 V: That is the e.m.f.; some p.d. is lost inside the cell.
- 2.5 V: You added the lost volts instead of subtracting.
- 0.5 V: That is the lost volts, Ir.

questions.stem: The resistance of a metal wire
questions.explanation:
Hotter atoms vibrate more and obstruct the electrons, so a metal's resistance rises with temperature.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- decreases as its temperature rises: That is true of semiconductors such as thermistors.
- does not depend on temperature: Metal resistance rises with temperature.
- decreases as its length increases: Resistance increases with length.

papers.title: Resistors and Circuit Analysis: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on resistors and circuit analysis, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel. What is their combined resistance?
questions.explanation:
$R = \dfrac{6 \times 3}{6 + 3} = 2\ \Omega$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 9 Ω: That is the series value.
- 4.5 Ω: You averaged the resistances.
- 18 Ω: You multiplied without dividing by the sum.

questions.stem: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω are in series across a 20 V supply. What is the current?
questions.explanation:
$R = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10\ \Omega$; $I = \dfrac{20}{10} = 2\ \text{A}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 20.7 A: You used the parallel combination; in series the resistances add.
- 200 A: You multiplied V by R.
- 10 A: That is the total resistance in ohms.

questions.stem: A 4 Ω resistor is connected in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 3 Ω resistors across a 12 V supply of negligible internal resistance. What is the total current?
questions.explanation:
Parallel pair: $\dfrac{6 \times 3}{9} = 2\ \Omega$. Total $= 4 + 2 = 6\ \Omega$. $I = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2\ \text{A}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.92 A: You added all three resistances in series.
- 3 A: You left out the parallel pair.
- 6 A: You used only the parallel pair (2 Ω).

questions.stem: A current of 3 A divides between resistors of 2 Ω and 4 Ω in parallel. What current flows through the 2 Ω resistor?
questions.explanation:
$I_2 = I \times \dfrac{R_4}{R_2 + R_4} = 3 \times \dfrac{4}{6} = 2\ \text{A}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1 A: That is the current in the 4 Ω resistor; the smaller resistor carries more.
- 1.5 A: The current does not divide equally.
- 3 A: The current is shared between the two branches.

questions.stem: In a metre bridge, a known resistance of 10 Ω is in the right-hand gap and the balance point is 40 cm from the left end. What is the unknown resistance in the left gap?
questions.explanation:
$\dfrac{X}{10} = \dfrac{40}{60} \Rightarrow X = 6.67\ \Omega$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 15 Ω: You inverted the ratio: X/R = l/(100 − l).
- 4 Ω: Use the ratio of the two lengths, 40/60, not 40/100.
- 25 Ω: You divided 10 by 0.4.

questions.stem: A potentiometer is preferred to a voltmeter for measuring the e.m.f. of a cell because, at balance, it
questions.explanation:
With no current drawn, there is no 'lost volts' in the cell, so the true e.m.f. is measured.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- has a very low resistance: The key point is that no current is drawn at balance.
- is always more sensitive than a galvanometer: It uses a galvanometer to find balance.
- adds to the e.m.f. of the cell: It measures the e.m.f.; it does not change it.

options.label: B
options.content: is always more sensitive than a galvanometer

options.label: C
options.content: adds to the e.m.f. of the cell

options.label: D
options.content: draws no current from the cell

questions.stem: To convert a galvanometer into an ammeter, connect
questions.explanation:
A low-resistance shunt in parallel carries most of the current, extending the range.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a large resistance in series with it: That converts it into a voltmeter.
- a small resistance in series with it: Most of the current must bypass the galvanometer, so the shunt goes in parallel.
- a large resistance in parallel with it: A large parallel resistance would carry little current.

options.label: A
options.content: a small resistance (shunt) in parallel with it

options.label: B
options.content: a large resistance in series with it

options.label: C
options.content: a small resistance in series with it

options.label: D
options.content: a large resistance in parallel with it

questions.stem: A galvanometer of resistance 20 Ω gives full-scale deflection at 2 mA. What series resistance converts it into a voltmeter reading up to 10 V?
questions.explanation:
$R = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G = \dfrac{10}{0.002} - 20 = 5000 - 20 = 4980\ \Omega$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 5000 Ω: You forgot to subtract the galvanometer's own 20 Ω.
- 5020 Ω: You added the galvanometer's resistance instead of subtracting it.
- 20 Ω: That is the galvanometer's resistance.

papers.title: Electric Energy and Power: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on electric energy and power, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: An electric iron draws 4 A from a 240 V supply. What is its power?
questions.explanation:
$P = VI = 240 \times 4 = 960\ \text{W}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 60 W: You divided the voltage by the current.
- 244 W: You added the voltage and current.
- 3840 W: You used P = I²V.

questions.stem: How many joules are there in one kilowatt-hour?
questions.explanation:
$1\ \text{kWh} = 1000\ \text{W} \times 3600\ \text{s} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.06 × 10⁶ J: You used 60 s instead of 3600 s.
- 0.0036 × 10⁶ J: You used 1 W instead of 1 kW (1000 W).
- 1.0 × 10⁶ J: A kilowatt-hour is power × time: 1000 W × 3600 s.

questions.stem: A 2 kW heater is used for 3 hours a day for 10 days. If one unit (kWh) costs NLe 2.00, what is the cost in leones (NLe)?
questions.explanation:
Energy $= 2 \times 3 \times 10 = 60$ kWh. Cost $= 60 \times 2.00 = $ NLe 120.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 60: You worked out the energy (60 kWh) but did not multiply by the price.
- 12: That is the cost for one day only.
- 120000: You used 2000 W instead of 2 kW.

questions.stem: What is the resistance of a lamp rated 240 V, 60 W when working normally?
questions.explanation:
$R = \dfrac{V^2}{P} = \dfrac{240^2}{60} = 960\ \Omega$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4 Ω: You divided V by P; R = V²/P.
- 0.25 Ω: That is the current, P/V.
- 14400 Ω: You multiplied V by P.

questions.stem: A lamp rated 240 V, 100 W is connected to a 120 V supply. What power does it use (resistance constant)?
questions.explanation:
$R = \dfrac{240^2}{100} = 576\ \Omega$; $P = \dfrac{120^2}{576} = 25\ \text{W}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 50 W: Power is proportional to V², so halving V quarters the power.
- 100 W: The rated power applies only at the rated voltage.
- 400 W: You inverted the ratio; the power falls when the voltage falls.

questions.stem: If the current through a resistor is tripled, by what factor does the rate of heat production change?
questions.explanation:
$P = I^2R$: tripling $I$ multiplies the power by $3^2 = 9$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 3: Heat production depends on I², not I.
- 6: 3² = 9, not 2 × 3.
- 27: It depends on I², not I³.

questions.stem: Electrical power is transmitted over long distances at high voltage in order to
questions.explanation:
For a given power P = VI, a higher voltage means a smaller current, and the heating loss I²R falls sharply.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increase the current in the cables: High voltage gives a small current for the same power.
- make the electricity travel faster: The voltage does not change the speed of transmission.
- increase the resistance of the cables: The cable resistance is fixed by their material and size.

options.label: A
options.content: increase the current in the cables

options.label: C
options.content: increase the resistance of the cables

options.label: D
options.content: reduce the current and so reduce I²R energy losses in the cables

questions.stem: Nichrome is used for the heating elements of electric kettles because it has
questions.explanation:
High resistivity gives the needed resistance; a high melting point and resistance to oxidation let it glow red hot.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a low resistivity and a low melting point: A low melting point would make it melt.
- a low resistivity: High resistivity is needed for heating with a reasonable length of wire.
- magnetic properties: Magnetism is irrelevant to heating elements.

options.label: A
options.content: a high resistivity and a high melting point

options.label: B
options.content: a low resistivity and a low melting point

papers.title: Electrolysis: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on electrolysis, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In electrolysis, positive ions move towards the
questions.explanation:
Positive ions (cations) are attracted to the negative electrode, the cathode.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- anode: The anode is positive, so it repels positive ions.
- electrolyte surface: Ions move towards the electrodes.
- battery: Ions stay in the electrolyte; electrons flow in the wires.

questions.stem: To electroplate a spoon with silver, the spoon should be made the
questions.explanation:
Silver ions from the electrolyte are deposited on the cathode (the spoon); a silver anode replaces them.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- anode, in a solution of a silver salt: Metal ions are deposited on the cathode, not the anode.
- cathode, in pure water: Pure water contains no silver ions.
- anode, in a copper sulphate solution: Copper sulphate would deposit copper, and on the cathode.

options.label: A
options.content: cathode, in a solution of a silver salt

options.label: B
options.content: anode, in a solution of a silver salt

options.label: D
options.content: anode, in a copper sulphate solution

questions.stem: A current of 2 A passes through copper sulphate solution for 1000 s. What mass of copper is deposited? (e.c.e. of copper = 3.3 × 10⁻⁷ kg C⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
$m = zIt = 3.3 \times 10^{-7} \times 2 \times 1000 = 6.6 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{kg} = 0.66\ \text{g}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.33 g: You used 1 A instead of 2 A.
- 0.00066 g: That is the mass in kilograms; the options are in grams.
- 6.6 g: Check the powers of ten: 3.3 × 10⁻⁷ × 2000 = 6.6 × 10⁻⁴ kg = 0.66 g.

questions.stem: During electrolysis of copper sulphate with copper electrodes, the colour of the solution
questions.explanation:
Copper dissolves from the anode as fast as it is deposited on the cathode, so the concentration stays constant.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- gradually fades: That happens with inert (platinum or carbon) electrodes, when copper ions are removed.
- becomes darker blue: The concentration of copper ions stays the same.
- turns green: No new substance colours the solution.

questions.stem: Faraday's first law of electrolysis states that the mass of a substance liberated is proportional to
questions.explanation:
$m = zQ = zIt$: mass ∝ charge passed.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the voltage across the electrodes: Mass depends on the charge (It), not the voltage.
- the area of the electrodes: Electrode area does not set the mass deposited.
- the temperature of the electrolyte: Temperature is not in Faraday's law.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a secondary (rechargeable) cell?
questions.explanation:
A lead–acid accumulator can be recharged by passing current through it in the reverse direction.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Leclanché dry cell: Dry cells are primary cells; they cannot be recharged.
- simple voltaic cell: This is a primary cell.
- Daniell cell: This is a primary cell.

questions.stem: Polarisation in a simple cell is caused by
questions.explanation:
Hydrogen bubbles on the copper raise the internal resistance and set up a back e.m.f.; a depolariser removes them.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- impurities in the zinc plate: That causes local action.
- the acid becoming too concentrated: Polarisation is due to hydrogen on the positive plate.
- the zinc plate dissolving: Zinc dissolving is the normal action of the cell.

options.label: A
options.content: bubbles of hydrogen collecting on the copper plate

questions.stem: How long must a current of 0.5 A flow to deposit 0.56 g of silver? (e.c.e. of silver = 1.12 × 10⁻⁶ kg C⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
$t = \dfrac{m}{zI} = \dfrac{0.56 \times 10^{-3}}{1.12 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.5} = 1000\ \text{s}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 500 s: You left out the current; t = m/(zI).
- 250 s: You multiplied by the current instead of dividing.
- 1000000 s: You used 0.56 kg instead of 0.56 × 10⁻³ kg.

papers.title: Magnets and Magnetic Fields: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on magnets and magnetic fields, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which material is used for the core of an electromagnet?
questions.explanation:
Soft iron magnetises strongly and loses its magnetism as soon as the current stops.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- steel: Steel keeps its magnetism; the electromagnet would not switch off.
- copper: Copper is not magnetic.
- aluminium: Aluminium is not magnetic.

questions.stem: According to the domain theory, a magnet is saturated when
questions.explanation:
Once every domain is aligned, the magnet cannot be made any stronger.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- its domains point in random directions: That describes an unmagnetised material.
- it has been heated strongly: Heating destroys the alignment.
- half its domains are aligned: Saturation means all of them are aligned.

options.label: A
options.content: all its domains are aligned in the same direction

options.label: B
options.content: its domains point in random directions

questions.stem: The best way to demagnetise a magnet is to
questions.explanation:
The reversing field of a.c., gradually reduced, leaves the domains in random directions.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- place it in a solenoid carrying direct current: Direct current magnetises; it does not demagnetise.
- store it with a keeper: Keepers preserve magnetism.
- stroke it with another magnet: Stroking magnetises.

options.label: A
options.content: place it in a solenoid carrying direct current

options.label: D
options.content: place it in a solenoid carrying alternating current and slowly withdraw it

questions.stem: Outside a bar magnet, magnetic field lines run
questions.explanation:
By convention, field lines leave the N pole and enter the S pole outside the magnet.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- from the south pole to the north pole: That is the direction inside the magnet.
- in circles round the middle of the magnet: That describes the field of a straight current-carrying wire.
- parallel to the magnet from end to end: They curve from pole to pole.

options.label: A

questions.stem: The angle between the Earth's magnetic field and the horizontal at a place is called the angle of
questions.explanation:
The angle of dip is 90° at the magnetic poles and 0° at the magnetic equator.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- declination: Declination is the angle between true north and magnetic north.
- incidence: That is a term from optics.
- deviation: That is a term from prisms.

questions.stem: A neutral point in a magnetic field is a point where
questions.explanation:
At a neutral point the fields of the magnets (and the Earth) cancel, so a compass shows no particular direction.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the field is strongest: At a neutral point the fields cancel.
- only north poles exist: Poles always come in pairs.
- the field lines cross: Field lines never cross.

options.label: A
options.content: the resultant magnetic field is zero

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-magnetic material?
questions.explanation:
Brass (copper and zinc) is not attracted by a magnet.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- nickel: Nickel is ferromagnetic.
- cobalt: Cobalt is ferromagnetic.
- steel: Steel is magnetic (used for permanent magnets).

questions.stem: Magnets are stored in pairs with soft-iron keepers in order to
questions.explanation:
The keepers complete a closed magnetic loop, keeping the domains aligned.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- make them stronger than saturation: No magnet can be stronger than saturation.
- demagnetise them: Keepers preserve magnetism.
- reverse their poles: Keepers do not reverse poles.

options.label: C
options.content: prevent them from losing their magnetism

questions.stem: The magnetic field lines around a long straight wire carrying a current are
questions.explanation:
Circles centred on the wire; the right-hand grip rule gives their direction.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- straight lines parallel to the wire: The field circles the wire.
- straight lines radiating from the wire: That describes the electric field of a charged wire.
- like those of a bar magnet: That describes a solenoid.

questions.stem: A wire 0.2 m long carries a current of 5 A at right angles to a magnetic field of 0.4 T. What is the force on it?
questions.explanation:
$F = BIL = 0.4 \times 5 \times 0.2 = 0.4\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2 N: You left out the length of the wire.
- 0.08 N: You left out the current.
- 1 N: You left out the magnetic field.

questions.stem: In Fleming's left-hand rule, the thumb points in the direction of the
questions.explanation:
First finger: Field; seCond finger: Current; thuMb: Motion (force).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- current: The second finger shows the current.
- magnetic field: The first finger shows the field.
- induced e.m.f.  
  That belongs to the right-hand (dynamo) rule.

questions.stem: The split-ring commutator in a d.c. motor
questions.explanation:
Reversing the coil current each half turn keeps the couple acting the same way, so the coil keeps rotating.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- keeps the current in the coil constant in direction: It reverses the coil current so the turning force stays in one direction.
- produces the magnetic field: The magnets produce the field.
- converts d.c. into a.c. for the supply: It does not change the supply.

questions.stem: Which change would NOT increase the strength of an electromagnet?
questions.explanation:
Copper is non-magnetic and does not strengthen the field.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increasing the current: More current gives a stronger field.
- increasing the number of turns: More turns give a stronger field.
- using a soft-iron core instead of air: Soft iron strengthens the field greatly.

options.label: C

questions.stem: Two long parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. The wires
questions.explanation:
Parallel currents in the same direction attract; in opposite directions they repel.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- repel each other: Currents in opposite directions repel.
- exert no force on each other: Each wire is in the other's magnetic field.
- rotate: They are pulled together, not rotated.

options.label: B

questions.stem: In an electric bell, the circuit is broken repeatedly because
questions.explanation:
When the armature is pulled to strike the gong, it leaves the contact screw, breaking the circuit; the spring pulls it back.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the battery runs down: The make-and-break is built into the bell.
- the gong breaks the circuit: The gong only makes the sound.
- the electromagnet reverses its poles: The electromagnet simply switches on and off.

options.label: A
options.content: the moving armature separates from the contact screw

questions.stem: The scale of a moving-coil galvanometer is uniform (linear) because
questions.explanation:
In a radial field the turning couple is proportional to the current, balanced by the spring couple proportional to deflection.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the hairsprings have no stiffness: The springs provide the restoring couple.
- the coil is made of soft iron: The coil is copper wire; the soft-iron cylinder helps make the field radial.
- it measures only alternating current: It measures d.c.

papers.title: Electromagnetic Induction: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on electromagnetic induction, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: When a magnet is held stationary inside a coil connected to a galvanometer, the galvanometer
questions.explanation:
Induction needs a changing magnetic flux; a stationary magnet gives none.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- deflects steadily in one direction: No change of flux means no induced e.m.f.
- deflects to and fro continuously: Only a changing flux induces an e.m.f.
- shows a maximum deflection: The magnet must move to induce a current.

questions.stem: Lenz's law is a consequence of the principle of conservation of
questions.explanation:
The induced current opposes the change, so work must be done to produce it: energy is conserved.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- charge: Charge conservation gives Kirchhoff's current rule.
- momentum: Momentum is not the basis of Lenz's law.
- mass: Mass conservation is unrelated.

questions.stem: The magnetic flux through a coil of 100 turns changes by 0.05 Wb in 0.25 s. What is the average induced e.m.f.?
questions.explanation:
$E = N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = 100 \times \dfrac{0.05}{0.25} = 20\ \text{V}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.2 V: You forgot to multiply by the 100 turns.
- 1.25 V: You multiplied by the time instead of dividing.
- 500 V: You divided the time by the flux change.

questions.stem: A rod 0.5 m long moves at 6 m s⁻¹ at right angles to a magnetic field of 0.2 T. What e.m.f. is induced across its ends?
questions.explanation:
$E = BLv = 0.2 \times 0.5 \times 6 = 0.6\ \text{V}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 15 V: You divided instead of multiplying (E = BLv).
- 1.2 V: You left out the length of 0.5 m.
- 0.1 V: You left out the speed.

questions.stem: The part of an a.c. generator that keeps the rotating coil connected to the external circuit is the
questions.explanation:
Slip rings turn with the coil, and the brushes press on them, giving an alternating output.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- split-ring commutator: A commutator makes the output d.c.
- field magnet: The magnet provides the field.
- soft-iron core: The core concentrates the field.

options.label: A
options.content: pair of slip rings with carbon brushes

questions.stem: Fleming's right-hand rule gives the direction of the
questions.explanation:
Right hand for generators: thuMb Motion, First finger Field, seCond finger induced Current.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- force on a current-carrying conductor: That is Fleming's left-hand rule.
- magnetic field around a straight wire: That is the right-hand grip rule.
- rotation of a motor: Motors use the left-hand rule.

options.label: B
options.content: induced current in a conductor moving in a magnetic field

options.label: C
options.content: magnetic field around a straight wire

questions.stem: Transformer cores are laminated in order to reduce
questions.explanation:
Thin insulated sheets break up the paths of eddy currents, reducing the heat they waste.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the number of turns needed: Laminating does not change the turns.
- the voltage output: Laminations reduce losses, not the output voltage.
- the frequency of the supply: The frequency is set by the supply.

questions.stem: The e.m.f. of a simple a.c. generator is greatest when the plane of the coil is
questions.explanation:
With the coil parallel to the field, its sides cut the field lines fastest.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- perpendicular to the magnetic field: Then the sides move along the field lines and the e.m.f. is zero.
- at 45° to the magnetic field: The e.m.f. is greater at 0° (parallel).
- stationary: No motion means no induced e.m.f.

papers.title: Alternating Current and Transformers: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on alternating current and transformers, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The peak value of an alternating current is 10 A. What is its r.m.s. value?
questions.explanation:
$I_{rms} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{10}{1.414} = 7.07\ \text{A}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 14.14 A: You multiplied by √2; r.m.s. = peak ÷ √2.
- 5 A: You halved the peak value.
- 20 A: That is the peak-to-peak value.

questions.stem: What is the period of a 50 Hz alternating supply?
questions.explanation:
$T = \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{50} = 0.02\ \text{s}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 50 s: That is the frequency, not the period.
- 0.2 s: 1/50 = 0.02, not 0.2.
- 0.01 s: That is the time for half a cycle.

questions.stem: A transformer has 1000 primary turns and 50 secondary turns. If the primary voltage is 240 V, what is the secondary voltage?
questions.explanation:
$V_s = V_p\dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = 240 \times \dfrac{50}{1000} = 12\ \text{V}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4800 V: You inverted the turns ratio; this is a step-down transformer.
- 240 V: The voltage changes in proportion to the turns.
- 0.208 V: You divided 50 by 240.

questions.stem: An ideal transformer steps 240 V down to 12 V. If the secondary current is 2 A, what is the primary current?
questions.explanation:
$I_p = \dfrac{V_sI_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{12 \times 2}{240} = 0.1\ \text{A}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 40 A: You inverted the ratio; stepping the voltage down steps the current up, so the primary current is smaller.
- 2 A: The currents are not equal: VpIp = VsIs.
- 24 A: That is the power in watts (VsIs), not the primary current.

questions.stem: A transformer takes 2 A from a 240 V supply and delivers 9 A at 48 V. What is its efficiency?
questions.explanation:
$\eta = \dfrac{48 \times 9}{240 \times 2} \times 100\% = \dfrac{432}{480} \times 100\% = 90\%$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 111.1 %: You divided input by output.
- 0.9 %: You found the ratio but did not multiply by 100.
- 20 %: You compared the voltages only: 48/240.

questions.stem: A transformer does not work on a steady d.c. supply because
questions.explanation:
Mutual induction needs a changing flux; a steady d.c. gives a constant flux, so nothing is induced in the secondary.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- d.c. has no voltage: d.c. does have a voltage.
- the core would melt: The core does not melt.
- d.c. cannot flow in copper wire: d.c. flows easily in copper.

options.label: A
options.content: a steady current produces no changing magnetic flux

options.label: D
options.content: d.c. cannot flow in copper wire

questions.stem: The r.m.s. value of an alternating current is defined as the
questions.explanation:
The r.m.s. value is the 'effective' value: the d.c. with the same heating effect.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- average of all the values over a cycle: The simple average over a whole cycle is zero.
- maximum value of the current: That is the peak value.
- value at the start of the cycle: That value is zero for a sine wave starting at 0.

options.label: A
options.content: average of all the values over a cycle

options.label: B
options.content: steady direct current that produces the same heating effect in a resistor

options.label: D
options.content: value at the start of the cycle

questions.stem: A 230 V r.m.s. supply is connected to a 46 Ω heater. What is the average power?
questions.explanation:
$P = \dfrac{V_{rms}^2}{R} = \dfrac{230^2}{46} = 1150\ \text{W}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 5 W: That is the r.m.s. current, not the power.
- 2300 W: You used the peak voltage (≈325 V) squared — that gives twice the average power.
- 10580 W: You multiplied V by R.

papers.title: Domestic Electricity and Safety: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on domestic electricity and safety, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In modern wiring, the live wire is coloured
questions.explanation:
Live = brown, neutral = blue, earth = green/yellow.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- blue: Blue is the neutral wire.
- green and yellow: Green and yellow is the earth wire.
- black: Black was the old colour for neutral.

questions.stem: Switches and fuses are connected in the live wire so that
questions.explanation:
With the switch or fuse in the live, opening it leaves the appliance at a safe potential.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the neutral wire carries more current: The same current flows in live and neutral.
- the appliance uses less energy: The position of the switch does not change energy use.
- the earth wire is not needed: The earth wire is still needed for metal-cased appliances.

options.label: C
options.content: the earth wire is not needed

options.content: the appliance is disconnected from the high voltage when the switch is off or the fuse blows

questions.stem: A 920 W iron is used on a 230 V supply. What is its working current?
questions.explanation:
$I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{920}{230} = 4\ \text{A}$, so a 5 A fuse is suitable.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.25 A: You divided V by P; I = P/V.
- 211600 A: You multiplied P by V.
- 690 A: You subtracted the voltage from the power.

questions.stem: The earth wire of an electric kettle is connected to its
questions.explanation:
If a fault makes the case live, a large current flows to earth and blows the fuse, so the case cannot give a shock.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- heating element: The element is connected to live and neutral.
- switch: The switch is in the live wire.
- fuse: The fuse is in the live wire.

questions.stem: Appliances in a house are connected in parallel so that
questions.explanation:
In parallel, every appliance has the full supply voltage and its own switch.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- they share the mains voltage equally: That would happen in series, not parallel.
- the same current flows through each: That happens in series.
- one fuse can protect them all from a shock: Parallel wiring is about voltage and independent switching.

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.stem: When a person is receiving an electric shock, the first thing to do is to
questions.explanation:
Break the contact safely first (switch off, or use a dry wooden stick), then call for help and give first aid.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- pull them away with your bare hands: You would receive a shock as well.
- pour water on them: Water conducts and makes things worse.
- wait for the current to stop: Delay can be fatal.

options.label: A
options.content: pull them away with your bare hands

options.label: C
options.content: switch off the supply or separate them from it with a dry insulator

options.label: D

questions.stem: A fuse of too high a rating is dangerous because
questions.explanation:
The cable could then overheat and start a fire before the fuse blows.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- it melts too easily: A higher rating melts less easily.
- it increases the mains voltage: A fuse does not change the voltage.
- it wastes a lot of energy: The energy wasted in a fuse is tiny.

options.label: C
options.content: it wastes a lot of energy

options.label: D
options.content: it may not melt when a fault causes a large current

questions.stem: Six 60 W bulbs are replaced by six 10 W LED bulbs, each used 5 hours a day. How many kWh are saved in 30 days?
questions.explanation:
Power saved $= 6 \times (60 - 10) = 300$ W $= 0.3$ kW. Energy $= 0.3 \times 5 \times 30 = 45$ kWh.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 54 kWh: That is the energy used by the old bulbs, not the saving.
- 9 kWh: That is the energy used by the LEDs.
- 45000 kWh: You used watts instead of kilowatts.

papers.title: Atomic Structure and Spectra: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on atomic structure and spectra, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. This showed that
questions.explanation:
Most alpha particles met nothing, so most of the atom is empty; a few bounced back from a tiny dense nucleus.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the nucleus is negatively charged: The nucleus is positive (it repels alpha particles).
- electrons are heavier than protons: Electrons are much lighter.
- atoms are indivisible: The experiment revealed internal structure.

options.label: A
options.content: most of the atom is empty space

questions.stem: How many neutrons are there in the nucleus of ²³⁸₉₂U?
questions.explanation:
Neutrons $= A - Z = 238 - 92 = 146$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 92: That is the number of protons.
- 238: That is the total number of nucleons.
- 330: You added A and Z.

questions.stem: Isotopes of an element have the same number of
questions.explanation:
Same proton number (same element), different neutron number (different mass).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- neutrons but different numbers of protons: Different proton numbers would be different elements.
- nucleons: Isotopes differ in nucleon number.
- neutrons and protons: Then they would be identical nuclei.

questions.stem: An electron in a hydrogen atom falls from an energy level of −3.4 eV to −13.6 eV. What is the energy of the photon emitted?
questions.explanation:
$\Delta E = -3.4 - (-13.6) = 10.2\ \text{eV}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 17.0 eV: You added the energies; the photon energy is their difference.
- 13.6 eV: That is the ionisation energy from the ground state.
- 3.4 eV: That is the energy of the upper level only.

questions.stem: A line emission spectrum is produced by
questions.explanation:
Atoms in a low-pressure hot gas emit light only at wavelengths set by their energy levels: bright lines.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a hot solid such as a lamp filament: Hot solids give continuous spectra.
- white light passing through a prism: That gives a continuous spectrum.
- a cold gas in front of a white light source: That gives an absorption spectrum.

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.stem: When an electron in an atom absorbs energy and moves to a higher energy level, the atom is said to be
questions.explanation:
Raising an electron to a higher level is excitation; it later falls back, emitting a photon.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- ionised: Ionisation means the electron leaves the atom completely.
- in its ground state: The ground state is the lowest level.
- radioactive: Radioactivity concerns the nucleus.

questions.stem: A photon has an energy of 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is its energy in electronvolts? (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
questions.explanation:
$E = \dfrac{3.2 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 2\ \text{eV}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 5.12 eV: You multiplied (3.2 × 1.6) instead of dividing.
- 0.5 eV: You divided 1.6 by 3.2.
- 3.2 eV: You did not convert from joules.

questions.stem: In Bohr's model of the atom, electrons
questions.explanation:
Bohr proposed fixed energy levels; light is emitted only when an electron jumps between them.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- are embedded in a sphere of positive charge: That is Thomson's model.
- spiral continuously into the nucleus: Bohr's model was proposed to avoid this.
- are found inside the nucleus: Electrons are outside the nucleus.

options.label: B

papers.title: Photoelectric Effect and Wave-Particle Duality: practice set 1

questions.stem: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of the light (frequency unchanged and above threshold) increases the
questions.explanation:
More intense light means more photons, so more electrons; each photon's energy is unchanged.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- maximum kinetic energy of the electrons: That depends on the frequency, not the intensity.
- work function of the metal: The work function is a property of the metal.
- threshold frequency: The threshold frequency is fixed for the metal.

options.label: B

questions.stem: Photons of energy 5.0 eV fall on a metal of work function 3.2 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons?
questions.explanation:
$E_{k,max} = hf - W = 5.0 - 3.2 = 1.8\ \text{eV}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 8.2 eV: You added the work function; it must be subtracted.
- 5.0 eV: Part of the photon's energy is used to escape the metal.
- 1.56 eV: You divided the energies.

questions.stem: The work function of a metal is
questions.explanation:
The work function W is the minimum energy for an electron to escape; W = hf₀.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron: That is hf − W.
- the energy of the incident photon: That is hf.
- the frequency below which electrons are emitted: Below the threshold frequency no electrons are emitted.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.content: the energy of the incident photon

options.label: C
options.content: the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from its surface

options.label: D
options.content: the frequency below which electrons are emitted

questions.stem: The photoelectric effect provides evidence that light
questions.explanation:
Each photon gives its energy to one electron: evidence for the particle nature of light.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- is a transverse wave: Polarisation shows that.
- can be diffracted: Diffraction shows wave behaviour.
- travels in straight lines: Shadows show that.

questions.stem: A metal has a work function of 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is its threshold frequency? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
questions.explanation:
$f_0 = \dfrac{W}{h} = \dfrac{3.3 \times 10^{-19}}{6.6 \times 10^{-34}} = 5.0 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2 × 10¹⁴ Hz: You divided h by W; the threshold frequency is f₀ = W/h.
- 21.78 × 10¹⁴ Hz: You multiplied W by h instead of dividing.
- 50 × 10¹⁴ Hz: Check the powers of ten: 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ ÷ 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ = 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

questions.stem: The gradient of a graph of maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against the frequency of the light is
questions.explanation:
$E_k = hf - W$ is a straight line of gradient $h$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the work function: The work function is the (negative) intercept on the energy axis.
- the threshold frequency: The threshold frequency is the intercept on the frequency axis.
- the charge of the electron: That is not the gradient.

questions.stem: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron (mass 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) moving at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
questions.explanation:
$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 2.0 \times 10^{6}} = 3.64 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 7.29 × 10⁻¹⁰ m: You divided h by m and left out the speed; λ = h/mv.
- 1.82 × 10⁻¹⁰ m: That is the momentum mv (in 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹), not the wavelength.
- 0.364 × 10⁻¹⁰ m: Check the power of ten: the answer is 3.64 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

questions.stem: Electron diffraction by a thin graphite film shows that
questions.explanation:
Diffraction rings are a wave effect, confirming de Broglie's matter waves.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- electrons are positively charged: Electrons are negative.
- light consists of photons: The experiment concerns electrons, not light.
- graphite is a conductor: That is not what diffraction shows.

papers.title: X-rays and Cathode Rays: practice set 1

questions.stem: Thermionic emission is the emission of electrons from
questions.explanation:
Heating gives free electrons enough energy to escape from the metal surface.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a metal when light falls on it: That is the photoelectric effect.
- a radioactive nucleus: That is beta decay.
- a gas at low pressure: Thermionic emission is from hot metal surfaces.

questions.stem: Cathode rays are deflected by both electric and magnetic fields. This shows that they
questions.explanation:
Only charged particles are deflected by electric and magnetic fields; cathode rays are electrons.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- are electromagnetic waves: Electromagnetic waves are not deflected by fields.
- travel in straight lines: Deflection shows charge, not straight-line travel.
- have no mass: They have mass (they are electrons).

questions.stem: An electron is accelerated through a p.d. of 1000 V. What kinetic energy does it gain? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.explanation:
$E_k = eV = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1000 = 1.6 \times 10^{-16}\ \text{J}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.16 × 10⁻¹⁶ J: Check the power of ten: 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1000 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J.
- 16 × 10⁻¹⁶ J: Check the power of ten.
- 0.0016 × 10⁻¹⁶ J: You divided by 1000 instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: The target of an X-ray tube is made of tungsten mainly because tungsten
questions.explanation:
Most of the electrons' energy becomes heat at the target, so it must withstand very high temperatures.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- is a good insulator: Tungsten is a metal and conducts.
- is cheap and light: Tungsten is chosen for its melting point and high atomic number.
- is radioactive: Tungsten is not radioactive.

options.label: A
options.content: has a very high melting point

questions.stem: The penetrating power (hardness) of X-rays is increased by
questions.explanation:
A higher p.d. gives faster electrons, which produce higher-frequency, more penetrating X-rays.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increasing the filament current: That increases the intensity (number of X-rays), not their hardness.
- using a copper target: The target material is not the control for hardness.
- letting air into the tube: The tube must be evacuated.

options.label: B
options.content: increasing the accelerating p.d. across the tube

questions.stem: In a cathode-ray oscilloscope, the brightness of the spot is controlled by the
questions.explanation:
The grid's negative potential controls how many electrons pass, and so the brightness.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Y-plates: Y-plates deflect the beam vertically.
- X-plates: X-plates deflect the beam horizontally.
- fluorescent screen: The screen only glows where the beam hits.

questions.stem: X-rays are used to examine broken bones because they
questions.explanation:
Dense bone absorbs more X-rays than soft tissue, so it shows up as a pale shadow on the film.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- are deflected by bones: X-rays are not deflected by matter in this way.
- are reflected by flesh: Flesh lets most X-rays through.
- make bones fluoresce: The image is formed on film or a detector behind the patient.

options.label: D
options.content: are absorbed more by bone than by soft tissue

questions.stem: An X-ray tube operates at 50 kV. What is the minimum wavelength of the X-rays produced? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.explanation:
$\lambda_{min} = \dfrac{hc}{eV} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 5.0 \times 10^{4}} = 2.49 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 24.9 × 10⁻¹¹ m: You used 5 kV instead of 50 kV.
- 0.249 × 10⁻¹¹ m: You used 500 kV instead of 50 kV.
- 1.21 × 10⁻¹¹ m: That is the maximum frequency eV/h in 10¹⁹ Hz, not the wavelength.

papers.title: Radioactivity and Nuclear Physics: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on radioactivity and nuclear physics, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which radiation is the most penetrating?
questions.explanation:
Gamma rays are uncharged electromagnetic waves; only thick lead or concrete reduces them.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- alpha particles: Alpha particles are stopped by paper.
- beta particles: Beta particles are stopped by a few mm of aluminium.
- all are equally penetrating: They differ greatly in penetration.

questions.stem: An alpha particle is identical to
questions.explanation:
An alpha particle is $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$: two protons and two neutrons.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- an electron: That is a beta particle.
- a photon: Gamma rays are photons.
- a hydrogen atom: An alpha particle has 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

questions.stem: A radioactive sample has a half-life of 4 days. What fraction of it remains after 12 days?
questions.explanation:
$\dfrac{12}{4} = 3$ half-lives; fraction $= \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \tfrac{1}{8}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.333: 12 days is three half-lives: (1/2)³ = 1/8, not 1/3.
- 0.25: That is the fraction after two half-lives (8 days).
- 0.167: You divided by 2 × 3 instead of 2³.

questions.stem: The activity of a source falls from 640 to 80 counts per minute in 30 minutes. What is its half-life?
questions.explanation:
$640 \to 320 \to 160 \to 80$: three half-lives in 30 min, so $T_{1/2} = 10$ min.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 15 min: 640 → 80 is three halvings, not two.
- 3.75 min: You divided 30 by 8 (the ratio) instead of by the number of half-lives.
- 30 min: That is the total time for three half-lives.

questions.stem: When a nucleus emits a beta particle, its
questions.explanation:
A neutron becomes a proton (Z + 1) and an electron is emitted; A stays the same.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- proton number decreases by 2 and nucleon number decreases by 4: That is alpha decay.
- proton number and nucleon number are both unchanged: That is gamma emission.
- nucleon number increases by 1: The nucleon number does not change in beta decay.

options.label: A
options.content: proton number decreases by 2 and nucleon number decreases by 4

options.label: B
options.content: proton number and nucleon number are both unchanged

options.label: C
options.content: proton number increases by 1 and its nucleon number is unchanged

questions.stem: A nucleus ²²⁶₈₈Ra emits an alpha particle. What is the nucleon number of the daughter nucleus?
questions.explanation:
Alpha decay: $A$ falls by 4: $226 - 4 = 222$ (and $Z$ falls to 86).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 224: Alpha emission removes 4 nucleons, not 2.
- 226: Alpha emission changes the nucleon number.
- 86: That is the new proton number.

questions.stem: How much energy is released when 2 × 10⁻³ kg of mass is converted completely into energy? (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
$E = mc^2 = 2 \times 10^{-3} \times (3.0 \times 10^{8})^2 = 1.8 \times 10^{14}\ \text{J}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.6 × 10¹⁴ J: You squared only the 10⁸, not the 3: (3.0 × 10⁸)² = 9.0 × 10¹⁶.
- 0.9 × 10¹⁴ J: You used ½mc²; the equation is E = mc².
- 18 × 10¹⁴ J: Check the power of ten: 2 × 10⁻³ × 9 × 10¹⁶ = 1.8 × 10¹⁴ J.

questions.stem: In a nuclear reactor, the control rods
questions.explanation:
Boron or cadmium control rods absorb neutrons; lowering them slows the reaction.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- slow down the neutrons: That is the job of the moderator.
- carry heat away to the turbines: That is the coolant.
- provide the nuclear fuel: The fuel is uranium in the fuel rods.

options.label: B
options.content: carry heat away to the turbines

options.label: D
options.content: absorb neutrons to control the rate of the chain reaction

papers.title: Semiconductors and Electronics: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on semiconductors and electronics, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The majority charge carriers in an n-type semiconductor are
questions.explanation:
A pentavalent donor gives a free electron, so electrons are the majority carriers.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- holes: Holes are the majority carriers in p-type material.
- protons: Protons do not move in a solid.
- positive ions: Ions are fixed in the crystal lattice.

questions.stem: A p-type semiconductor is made by doping pure silicon with
questions.explanation:
A trivalent acceptor leaves a missing electron (a hole) in the bonds.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a pentavalent element such as phosphorus: That makes n-type material.
- more silicon: Pure silicon is intrinsic.
- copper: Copper is not used as a dopant for p-type silicon.

options.label: A
options.content: a pentavalent element such as phosphorus

options.label: B
options.content: a trivalent element such as boron

questions.stem: A p-n junction diode conducts a large current when
questions.explanation:
Forward bias narrows the depletion layer, and above about 0.6 V a large current flows.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- it is reverse-biased: Reverse bias widens the depletion layer and blocks current.
- the n-side is connected to the positive terminal: That is reverse bias.
- no voltage is applied: A p.d. of about 0.6 V forward is needed.

options.label: B
options.content: the n-side is connected to the positive terminal

options.label: C
options.content: it is forward-biased, with the p-side connected to the positive terminal

questions.stem: The process of converting a.c. into d.c. is called
questions.explanation:
Diodes rectify a.c. by letting current through in one direction only.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- amplification: Amplification makes signals larger.
- induction: Induction produces an e.m.f. from a changing flux.
- modulation: Modulation puts a signal onto a carrier wave.

questions.stem: As the temperature of a pure semiconductor rises, its resistance
questions.explanation:
Heating frees more electrons and holes, so a semiconductor's resistance falls.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increases: That is the behaviour of metals.
- stays the same: More charge carriers are released when it is heated.
- becomes infinite: It conducts better when hot.

questions.stem: A transistor has a base current of 40 μA and a collector current of 6 mA. What is its current gain?
questions.explanation:
$\beta = \dfrac{I_C}{I_B} = \dfrac{6 \times 10^{-3}}{40 \times 10^{-6}} = 150$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.0067: You divided the base current by the collector current.
- 0.15: You did not convert mA and μA to the same unit.
- 240: You multiplied the two numbers.

questions.stem: The output of a NOR gate is 1 only when
questions.explanation:
NOR = NOT OR: OR is 0 only when both inputs are 0, so NOR is then 1.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- both inputs are 1: Then the OR output is 1, so NOR gives 0.
- either input is 1: Any input of 1 makes the NOR output 0.
- the inputs are different: That describes an exclusive-OR (XOR) gate.

questions.stem: A large capacitor is connected across the output of a rectifier in order to
questions.explanation:
The capacitor charges at each peak and discharges between peaks, filling in the gaps.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increase the frequency: The capacitor does not raise the frequency.
- convert d.c. back into a.c.  
  It smooths the d.c.
- protect the diode from heat: It stores charge at the peaks and releases it between them.

options.label: C
options.content: smooth the output into a steadier d.c.

papers.title: Practical Physics Skills: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on practical physics skills, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: When a question says 'plot V against I', the quantity on the vertical axis should be
questions.explanation:
'Plot y against x': the first quantity (V) is on the vertical axis.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- I: The first-named quantity goes on the vertical (y) axis.
- V × I: Plot the measured quantities, not their product.
- time: Time is not part of this graph.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a good precaution when timing a simple pendulum?
questions.explanation:
Timing many oscillations reduces the effect of reaction time on each period.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Take readings carefully.  
  This is too vague to earn credit.
- Use a very heavy bob only.  
  The mass of the bob does not affect the period, and this is not a timing precaution.
- Swing the bob through a very large angle.  
  A large angle makes the motion depart from SHM.

options.label: A
options.content: Time 20 oscillations and calculate the average period.

options.label: C
options.content: Use a very heavy bob only.

options.label: D
options.content: Swing the bob through a very large angle.

questions.stem: A length is recorded as (50.0 ± 0.1) cm. What is the percentage error?
questions.explanation:
Percentage error $= \dfrac{0.1}{50.0} \times 100\% = 0.2\%$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.1 %: That is the absolute error in cm, not the percentage.
- 0.002 %: You found the fractional error but did not multiply by 100.
- 2.0 %: 0.1 ÷ 50 × 100 = 0.2%, not 2%.

questions.stem: The percentage error in measuring the period T of a pendulum is 1.5%. What is the percentage error in T²?
questions.explanation:
For $T^2$, multiply the percentage error by 2: $2 \times 1.5\% = 3\%$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.5 %: When a quantity is squared, its percentage error doubles.
- 2.25 %: You squared the percentage error; multiply it by the power instead.
- 0.75 %: You halved instead of doubling.

questions.stem: To find the gradient of a straight-line graph accurately, you should
questions.explanation:
A large triangle on the best-fit line reduces the error in reading Δy and Δx.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- use the first two plotted points from the table: They may not lie exactly on the best-fit line.
- use a very small triangle near the origin: A small triangle increases the percentage reading error.
- divide the last y-value by the last x-value: That is correct only for a line through the origin, and it ignores the best fit.

options.label: A
options.content: use the first two plotted points from the table

options.label: B
options.content: use a large right-angled triangle drawn on the line

options.label: C
options.content: use a very small triangle near the origin

options.label: D
options.content: divide the last y-value by the last x-value

questions.stem: Parallax error when reading a scale is avoided by
questions.explanation:
Viewing perpendicularly to the scale removes the apparent shift caused by viewing at an angle.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- reading the scale from one side: That introduces parallax.
- using a longer scale: Scale length does not remove parallax.
- taking the reading quickly: Speed does not affect parallax.

options.label: A
options.content: reading the scale from one side

options.label: C
options.content: placing the eye directly in line with the reading, perpendicular to the scale

questions.stem: In the glass-block experiment, the refractive index is found from the gradient of a graph of
questions.explanation:
$\sin i = n\sin r$: a graph of sin i against sin r is a straight line of gradient n.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- i against r: Snell's law relates the sines, so i against r is not a straight line through the origin.
- sin r against i: Use the sines of both angles.
- 1/i against 1/r: That has no simple relation to n.

questions.stem: A graph of T² (s²) against l (m) for a pendulum has a gradient of 4.0 s² m⁻¹. What is g? (take π² = 9.87)
questions.explanation:
$T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{g}l$, so $g = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{\text{gradient}} = \dfrac{4 \times 9.87}{4.0} = 9.87\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4.0 m s⁻²: That is the gradient; g = 4π²/gradient.
- 0.101 m s⁻²: You inverted the relation: g = 4π² ÷ gradient.
- 2.47 m s⁻²: You used π² instead of 4π².
